explanations.answer: He wishes it were burning already
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Jesus says, "I have come to ignite a fire on the earth, and how I wish it were already kindled!" (Luke 12:49). The wish is right there in the verse. I know a little about wishing for things to hurry up, but mine is a cookie timer, and it has never once listened.

explanations.answer: He wishes it could wait a while
explanations.explanation: Nice thinking, friend, but the verse goes the other way. Jesus says, "how I wish it were already kindled!" (Luke 12:49). "Already" means He wishes it were burning now, not later. Nobody in this verse is asking for more time.

explanations.answer: He wishes it would go out soon
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. Jesus says He came to ignite the fire, and then, "how I wish it were already kindled!" (Luke 12:49). Kindled means lit, and He wishes that had already happened. The only time I ever wished a fire out was a batch I forgot about.

Calm and settled is a gentle thought, friend, but the text says the opposite. Jesus says, "But I have a baptism to undergo, and how distressed I am until it is accomplished!" (Luke 12:50). "Distressed" is the word He uses. I think this is a heavy line, so I'll let it sit just as it is.

That's right, baker, and the calm part is what makes it false. Jesus says, "But I have a baptism to undergo, and how distressed I am until it is accomplished!" (Luke 12:50). He says He is distressed until it is accomplished. I get jittery over a tray of cookies, so I won't compare. I'll just tell you what the verse says.

Division, baker. Jesus asks, "Do you think that I have come to bring peace to the earth? No, I tell you, but division." (Luke 12:51). He asks the question and answers it Himself, so no guessing is needed. It's a hard word, and I'd rather hand you the plain verse than dress it up.
Rest sounds lovely, friend. I've wanted some myself after a long day at the ovens. But rest isn't the word in the verse. Jesus says, "No, I tell you, but division." (Luke 12:51).

Healing is a good word, baker, but it isn't the one here. Jesus is answering whether He came to bring peace to the earth, and He says, "No, I tell you, but division." (Luke 12:51). Hold on to that word, because the next verse shows what it looks like inside one house (Luke 12:52).

True, baker. Jesus says households will be divided, "father against son and son against father" (Luke 12:53). It runs in both directions, and the verse keeps going with mothers and daughters too (Luke 12:53). I think this one hurts to hear, so I'll just say it plainly.

It's true, friend, even though it's hard to hear. Jesus says, "father against son and son against father" (Luke 12:53). The verse says it both ways, and then goes on to mother against daughter and daughter against mother (Luke 12:53). This is a heavy part, and I won't dress it up.

A shower, baker. Jesus says, "As soon as you see a cloud rising in the west, you say, ‘A shower is coming,’ and that is what happens." (Luke 12:54). They see the cloud, make the call, and the rain shows up. Those folks could have run the weather report for the whole town.

Frost is a chilly guess, friend, but that's not the call. Jesus says the crowds say, ‘A shower is coming,’ and that is what happens (Luke 12:54). A shower means rain, not ice. Frost would have had everybody digging out scarves for nothing.

A windstorm has some drama to it, baker, but the cloud in the west brings a different call. Jesus says they say, ‘A shower is coming’ (Luke 12:54). Wind does show up in the very next verse, but there the south wind means heat (Luke 12:55).

Hot, baker. Jesus says, "And when the south wind blows, you say, ‘It will be hot,’ and it is." (Luke 12:55). That's two calls in a row, first the shower, then the heat (Luke 12:54). Heat is the one thing I never need a forecast for, since I live next to an oven.

Cold is the opposite of the call here, friend. Jesus says the crowds say, ‘It will be hot,’ and it is (Luke 12:55). The verse says it turned out just as they said. Cold would have had everyone in sweaters, sweating.

Stormy is a fun guess, baker, but it isn't the south wind's call. Jesus says they say, ‘It will be hot,’ and it is (Luke 12:55). The rain call belongs to the cloud in the west, where the crowds say a shower is coming (Luke 12:54).

The present time, baker. Jesus says, "You know how to interpret the appearance of the earth and sky. Why don’t you know how to interpret the present time?" (Luke 12:56). The crowds are good at clouds and wind, and He asks why they can't read the time they're living in. Me, I can look out my bakery window and still get rained on.

Scrolls are a thoughtful guess, friend, but this verse doesn't mention them. Jesus says, "Why don’t you know how to interpret the present time?" (Luke 12:56). On one side is the earth and sky, and on the other is the present time. There are no scrolls in this verse.

Dreams would be a fun thing to interpret, baker, but they aren't in this verse. Jesus says, "You know how to interpret the appearance of the earth and sky. Why don’t you know how to interpret the present time?" (Luke 12:56). The thing they can't read is the present time. I can barely interpret my own dreams, so I'm no help there.

That's the opposite of what the verse says, friend. Jesus asks, "And why don’t you judge for yourselves what is right?" (Luke 12:57). The word is "yourselves," so there's no passing it to someone else. It comes right after He asks why they can't interpret the present time (Luke 12:56).

False, baker. Jesus asks, "And why don’t you judge for yourselves what is right?" (Luke 12:57). The word is "yourselves," so the judging is theirs to do. Even my taste testing is a job I can't hand off.

Reconcile, baker. Jesus says, "Make every effort to reconcile with your adversary while you are on your way to the magistrate." (Luke 12:58). Then He warns, "he may drag you off to the judge" (Luke 12:58). Every effort is a lot of effort, more than I put into finding my own spatula.

Arguing is the natural pull, friend, but it isn't the word. Jesus says, "Make every effort to reconcile with your adversary while you are on your way to the magistrate." (Luke 12:58). To reconcile is to make things right between you two. Arguing the whole way there would just make for a long walk.

Competing sounds like a sport, baker, but this isn't a contest. Jesus says, "Make every effort to reconcile with your adversary while you are on your way to the magistrate." (Luke 12:58). The verse says to reconcile, and it never says to win. There are no trophies at the magistrate's door.

An early release would be nice, friend, but the verse says otherwise. Jesus says, "I tell you, you will not get out until you have paid the very last penny." (Luke 12:59). "Until" is the key word, and the last penny is the finish line. I was sold for a quarter at a closing bakery, so I know every penny counts.

False, baker. Jesus says, "I tell you, you will not get out until you have paid the very last penny." (Luke 12:59). No getting out early, and the last penny is the mark. I was bought for a quarter, and even I wouldn't want to owe anybody a cent.
